clinicalPearls: A lymphocytic scarring (cicatricial) alopecia causing progressive band-like recession of the frontotemporal hairline, most often in postmenopausal women
Eyebrow loss is very common and may precede the scalp changes, and loss of body and limb hair also occurs
The recessed skin appears pale, atrophic and scarred with loss of follicular openings, often contrasting with the more sun-damaged skin behind the original hairline
Perifollicular erythema and follicular hyperkeratosis are seen at the advancing margin, sometimes with lonely hairs stranded within the scarred zone
It is regarded as a clinical variant of lichen planopilaris and shares its perifollicular lymphocytic inflammation on histology
Facial papules, involvement of the temples and occiput, and prominence of frontal veins may accompany more advanced disease

Management aims to halt progression with anti-inflammatory and antiandrogenic approaches such as topical or intralesional corticosteroids and 5-alpha-reductase inhibition, since regrowth in scarred areas is not achievable
reference.pathophysiology: Frontal fibrosing alopecia is a lymphocytic cicatricial alopecia regarded as a clinical variant of lichen planopilaris. A T-cell-mediated inflammatory attack is directed at the stem-cell region in the follicular bulge, leading to destruction of the follicle and its replacement by fibrous tissue. The predilection for the frontotemporal hairline and eyebrows, the postmenopausal peak, and reported links to hormonal and possibly environmental or contactant factors suggest a multifactorial aetiology, but once follicular stem cells are lost the hair loss is permanent.
additionalDifferentials: Traction alopecia, which is marginal, non-scarring early and has a tension history
Lichen planopilaris in its classic vertex or patchy form
Alopecia areata in an ophiasis pattern
Discoid lupus erythematosus of the scalp
additionalInvestigations: Trichoscopy showing perifollicular erythema and hyperkeratosis, loss of ostia and lonely hairs
Scalp biopsy from the active margin demonstrating perifollicular lymphocytic inflammation and fibrosis
Assessment of eyebrows and body hair for associated loss
Photographic and line-marking documentation to monitor the hairline over time
Screening for associated autoimmune or thyroid disease where indicated
redFlags: Rapidly advancing hairline recession threatening extensive permanent loss
Facial papules or marked eyebrow loss indicating active, progressive disease
Features suggesting overlap with discoid lupus requiring different management
reference.prognosis: The disease is chronic and slowly progressive with permanent hair loss in affected areas; treatment can stabilise or slow progression but cannot restore lost hair, although spontaneous stabilisation may eventually occur.
pitfalls: Mistaking the recession for androgenetic or traction alopecia and missing the scarring nature
Overlooking eyebrow loss as an early and important clue
Failing to biopsy the active margin, so a treatable inflammatory process is not confirmed
Promising regrowth in scarred skin, where follicles are irreversibly lost
management: Anti-inflammatory therapy to arrest progression, including topical and intralesional corticosteroids and topical calcineurin inhibitors applied to the active hairline margin
Systemic treatment with 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors such as finasteride or dutasteride as a mainstay, with hydroxychloroquine or oral retinoids in progressive disease
Explanation that treatment aims to stabilise or slow progression rather than regrow hair, since the scarring hair loss is permanent
Cosmetic and psychological support including eyebrow pencilling or tattooing, camouflage, and hair-restoration options once disease is quiescent
Photographic and hairline documentation with trichoscopy to monitor disease activity and treatment response
Screening for and management of associated autoimmune or thyroid disease, with sun protection of the exposed scarred skin
Dermatology follow-up to reassess activity and adjust therapy
